US President Donald Trump said he was not seeking further escalation with Iran following the midterm elections. "I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to," he said in an interview with CBS News' 60 Minutes. He also repeated his claim that Israel would not exist without US military strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities. Trump claimed the US had won the war and that Tehran was interested in reaching an agreement. "We would have had a deal except for this election," he said, suggesting the Democratic victory had complicated negotiations. Trump said a "great dislike" for Israel, public opposition to the war with Iran and rising gasoline prices were the primary reasons Republicans suffered sweeping losses in last week's midterm elections. - Israeli president tasks Eisenkot with forming new government Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Sunday tasked Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new government after parliamentary elections left his bloc and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance short of a majority. Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government under Israel’s Basic Law. Herzog can grant him up to 14 additional days if needed, according to the daily Yedioth Ahronoth. Herzog announced his decision to ask Eisenkot to form the next government on Saturday after consulting parliamentary factions. ​​​​​​​His office said factions representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended Eisenkot, while factions representing 46 backed Netanyahu. First held in Berlin in 1995, the annual summit provides a platform for countries party to the convention to assess progress in combating climate change, develop common solutions, and make decisions shaping global climate policies. Türkiye will preside over this year's conference, which runs on Nov. 9-20 and addresses key decisions on sustainable development and climate policies. items.title: Economic Update: Week of November 9, 2026 | Traders' Insight
items.excerpt: ## Growth Real GDP grew 3.4% SAAR in 3Q, accelerating from 2.2% in 2Q and exceeding expectations, as strong business investment and consumer spending outweighed a drag from net exports. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers rose 4.9%, while nonresidential investment surged 12.7%, supported by continued AI-related spending. Consumer spending rose 3.8%, and federal spending added nearly 1% to growth, while residential investment fell 3.3% amid demographic shifts and high mortgage rates. Looking ahead, growth may moderate as fiscal support fades and housing remains weak, though business investment should continue to provide support. Imports of AI-related hardware may keep net exports a drag, but with PCE inflation at 3.6%, the Fed may look to raise rates in December. ... ## Jobs The October jobs report showed payrolls rising by 165k, well above expectations of 70k, while August and September payrolls were revised higher by a combined 84k. Hiring was driven by professional and business services, health care and transportation and warehousing, helping private-sector payrolls rise by 159k. Government employment was relatively muted, adding just 6k jobs. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, while wage growth came in above expectations at 3.1% year-over-year, though it remained below headline inflation for the seventh consecutive month. For the Fed, a strengthening labor market leaves more room to focus on inflation. ... ## Inflation Headline CPI rose 0.6% m/m, the largest monthly increase since April, pushing the y/y rate to 3.7%, driven primarily by a further acceleration in energy prices. Core CPI again came in hotter than expected, rising 0.3% m/m compared to consensus estimates of 0.2%. Core inflation was led higher by several categories, including recreation, used cars and trucks, education and airline fares. Elsewhere, food prices were contained. With core CPI still elevated relative to the Fed’s target, the question on investors’ minds has now shifted from “Will the Fed hike rates?” to “How many times will the Fed hike rates?” ... At its September meeting, the Federal Reserve voted 10-2 to maintain the federal funds rate target range at 3.75-4.00%. The committee upgraded its growth assessment to “strong” from “solid,” but also noted the need for more information to assess the impact of last month’s rate hike, preserving the option to hike or hold in December. Economic strength outside of AI was also highlighted while the committee reaffirmed its commitment to returning to 2% inflation. Although markets are pricing in a December hike, upcoming inflation data will be key in determining whether it materializes.

items.title: The Fed - The Effect of Oil Prices on Core Inflation: Recent Evidence from the Advanced Economies
items.excerpt: November 09, 2026 ### The Effect of Oil Prices on Core Inflation: Recent Evidence from the Advanced Economies Andrea De Michelis, Musa Orak, Avani Pradhan, and Albert Queralto 1 Elevated oil prices and heightened geopolitical uncertainty have renewed interest in a longstanding policy question: do supply shocks like oil-price increases pose a transitory or a persistent threat to price stability? This note sheds light on this question by providing new evidence on whether the inflation process has changed. In an earlier note, De Michelis et al. (2024) documented that core inflation had become more inertial after the pandemic, implying that supply shocks might be expected to have more persistent effects if this greater inertia continued. This note updates those results using a similar methodology with data extended through the middle of this year and documents a second change in the inflation process: an increase in the pass-through from oil prices to core inflation. Because the post-pandemic period remains short, we estimate the model using a panel of five major advanced economies rather than data from a single country, which allows us to detect common shifts in persistence and pass-through more robustly. We find that the pass-through from oil prices to core inflation, which was statistically indistinguishable from zero before the pandemic, rose to an economically and statistically significant level afterwards. A horse race among nested specifications shows that allowing for stronger post-pandemic pass-through, on top of stronger persistence, delivers a marked improvement in our model's ability to track core inflation dynamics in recent years. Our estimated model implies that the recent rise in oil prices could significantly raise core inflation in the advanced economies over the next few years were the greater persistence and higher pass-through to continue. Finally, we use a structural global macroeconomic model to assess the broader implications of the changes in the inflation process, focusing on how these changes bear on the appropriate monetary policy response to supply shocks. Admittedly, our empirical results are derived using a reduced-form approach that cannot distinguish a structural change in the underlying inflation process from the possibility that global supply shocks have become more frequent, more persistent, or both. The results presented here depend on our specification and set of controls, and different specifications might yield different results. Relatedly, while our panel approach expands the information set by pooling together data across the major advanced economies, it does not allow us to control for some specific factors that have seemingly contributed to persistently elevated inflation in the U.S. because of the lack of comparable data in other countries. In addition, even if our results stem from a structural change reflecting, for instance, a shift in behavior of price setters, we cannot say whether this change will endure or reverse. These caveats notwithstanding, we view our results as suggestive of an upside risk to inflation. We also stress that the results shown here do not represent any official forecasts of inflation in the U.S. or foreign economies.

items.title: October CPI follows a month when gasoline drove over half of the rise in US prices | FinanceInTime
items.excerpt: ## One component carried September's jump The consumer price index for all urban consumers (CPI-U) rose 0.6% in September on a seasonally adjusted basis, the BLS said. Over the 12 months through September the all-items index rose 3.7% before seasonal adjustment, a larger increase than the 3.4% reported for the 12 months through August. That is an acceleration of 0.3 percentage point (computed). The BLS attributed much of the monthly move to fuel. The energy index increased 5.2% over the month, following a 2.1% increase in August, and the gasoline index rose 9.1% in September, "accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase." Over 12 months, the energy index was up in large part because gasoline rose 34.2%, the BLS said. FinanceInTime covered that release in a report on the gasoline-led rise. A rise that rests on one volatile component leaves a plain question for the next report: whether the component held its level, gave some of the increase back or kept climbing. ## Core prices were steadier than the headline The index for all items less food and energy, known as core, rose 0.3% in September, as it did in August. Core is the measure analysts use to look past swings in fuel and groceries. Two other parts of the basket were quieter than energy. The shelter index, which covers rent and the estimated rental value of owner-occupied homes, rose 0.4% in September after 0.3% in August, and was up 3.2% over the last year. The index for food was unchanged in September and was up 2.5% over the last year. Taken together, the September figures show a headline that moved on energy and a core index that moved at the same 0.3% pace in both months. The report does not say whether that pace will continue.

items.excerpt: Investing.com - U.S. consumer prices are estimated to have risen by 3.8% in the twelve months to October and 0.3% month-on-month, amid ongoing upward pressure from elevated energy costs caused by the Iran war, according to Truflation predictions. ... Stripping out volatile items like food and fuel, the so-called "core" gauge is seen standing at 2.8% year-on-year and 0.2% month-on-month, the alternative data provider said in a statement. "Headline inflation is moderating, but upstream inflation pipeline remains active. Energy and tariffs are supporting renewed goods inflation. The key risk heading into 2027 is whether rising supply costs spread into persistent core inflation before consumer price sensitivity and moderating labor costs can offset them," Truflation said. The group added that it expects "uneven inflation" through the end of the year and early into 2027, with heightened goods prices due to tariffs and input expenses partially offset by stable services costs. Levies are seen pushing retail prices higher, although grocery prices are anticipated to fall because of retailer discounting and improving supplies. Energy is still the "principal swing factor" for overall price gains, Truflation flagged. For October, the group projected a 20.7% rise in energy prices versus a year earlier, with gasoline in particular climbing 37.7%. Month-on-month, gas price growth is tipped to moderate to 0.3%.

items.title: Headlines for November 09, 2026
items.excerpt: ## Democrats Build on Sweeping Gains in Midterm Elections, Claiming 254 House Seats Nov 09, 2026 Democrats are continuing to build on their sweeping gains in last week’s midterm elections as votes continue to be counted. They can now claim 254 House seats, compared to 162 for Republicans, with 19 House races yet to be decided. Democrats will also control at least 30 governorships and will control both legislative chambers and the governor’s office in 23 states — up from 16 before the election. Democrats also broke Republican “trifectas” in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and in Texas, where 87-year-old Houston Democrat Senfronia Thompson says she has the votes to become the first woman and first Black speaker of the Texas House of Representatives. Retired Navy Vice Admiral Nancy Lacore, who was abruptly fired from her post as chief of the Navy Reserve by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in August 2025, won election to the House of Representatives, flipping a seat in South Carolina held by the GOP. According to Axios, the House is poised to impeach Hegseth this week. Meanwhile, Houston, Texas, Mayor John Whitmire announced Friday the city would start limiting the collaboration of local law enforcement with ICE during traffic stops. The announcement comes amid pressure from activists and as Republican Governor Greg Abbott prepares to leave office. Abbott previously threatened to revoke more than $110 million in public safety funding to Houston over a policy granting officers discretion over whether or not to contact ICE. Houston has seen mounting violent incidents involving ICE agents during traffic stops and car pursuits, including the fatal shooting of Mexican father Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July. This is Houston Mayor Whitmire. > Mayor John Whitmire: “This morning, I have directed the chief and HPD, through an executive order, that we will change our policy in regarding contact with ICE. I do this to begin a healing process, reduce fear and anxiety across our community. I also do this knowing that elections matter.” ## Trump Replaces White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller Nov 09, 2026 President Trump has replaced White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the chief architect of his mass deportation policy, days after Republicans lost control of Congress. In a statement, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Democratic Congressmember Robert Garcia, said, “Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down. Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families. Stephen Miller should lawyer up.” Attorney General Todd Blanche responded on Fox News that quote “Stephen Miller has a lawyer, it’s me”. This is Blanche on CNN.

items.title: Trump administration live updates: Congress returns with government funding atop the to-do list
items.excerpt: ## What to know today - CONGRESS IS BACK: Congress returns today for a lame-duck session after Democrats delivered a crushing defeat to Republicans in the midterm elections. The first order of business on the tall list of tasks is funding the government to avert a shutdown in December. - SENATE LEADERSHIP: A growing number of Republican senators are calling for a delay in their leadership elections tomorrow morning to discuss contenders' plans after the GOP's midterm losses. - TRUMP ON IMMIGRATION: President Donald Trump conceded in an interview on CBS News’ “60 Minutes” that his immigration policies were “too tough,” saying mass deportations hurt him in the midterm elections. - UNCALLED RACES: Vote counting continues in the Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi, where Democratic candidates Mary Peltola and Scott Colom narrowly lead their respective Republican opponents, Sens. Dan Sullivan and Cindy Hyde-Smith. ## Blanche says DOJ won't 'stop working with Congress' under Democratic majority Attorney General Todd Blanche said today that the Justice Department won't "stop working with Congress" under the incoming Democratic majority next year. At a press conference for an unrelated event in St. Louis, Missouri, Blanche was asked to pledge not to interference with congressional oversight. "The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it’s through subpoenas or letters — and so we’re not going to stop working with Congress or allowing them to conduct their oversight responsibilities and nothing I’ve said this weekend or in the past should suggest otherwise,” he said. Democrats have made clear since the election last week that they plan to conduct oversight investigations into Trump and the administration in the new Congress. During the first Trump administration, the president and officials often evaded congressional oversight probes and defied subpoenas under the Democratic majority at the time. ... ## Senate Republicans call for delay in tomorrow's leadership elections A group of Senate Republicans has sent a letter to the head of the Senate Republican Conference requesting “a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead” before it holds leadership elections. Doing otherwise would be "political malpractice," the letter, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said. It was also signed by Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, John Kennedy of Louisiana, and Rick Scott of Florida. The elections are currently scheduled for 9 a.m. ET tomorrow. In the letter to the conference chair, Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., the senators proposed they instead hold a discussion at the meeting. They proposed the conference "delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats." Separately, Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., posted on X this morning that “tomorrow is too soon” to elect Republican leadership in the Senate for the next Congress. “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here," Banks wrote. Sen. David McCormick, R-Pa., also posted ... Postponing the leadership election would require the support of a simple majority of the conference.

items.excerpt: ## Music U2: Carnaval De Luz When: 13 November After an almost ten year hiatus, Irish rockers U2 are back with their 16th studio album: 'Carnaval de Luz'. It marks 50 years since the band first formed in Dublin, with an eclectic 12-track collection that's fittingly reflective, matured, and at times existential. There's also a notable collaboration with the late country queen Dolly Parton, whose duet on 'torn' ended up being her final ever recording. Another highlight includes 'The Mirror Maker', a song written entirely about the Spanish singer Rosalía which, according to producer Jacknife Lee, took nearly 200 takes to get right. But eventually they found what they were looking for — hopefully fans will too. Bonus highlight: For a less mainstream vibe, California indie band Wavves are releasing their 11th studio album, 'Cherry Soda', on 13 November 2026.

items.excerpt: ### James Bond: Denis Villeneuve stops just short of naming the next 007 - What happened: Accepting his honour at LACMA’s Art+Film Gala in Los Angeles on Saturday 7 November, Villeneuve told the audience: “With the blessing of my new friends at Amazon, I will reveal to you tonight who will be the next James Bond. The new James Bond is…” before adding, “and I will stop right now because Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” The Hollywood Reporter reported. On the red carpet he told Variety he was having a “great time” with the casting but named no one - Where the search stands: Nobody has been cast. Deadline reports, citing insiders, that Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult took part in final screen tests. Amazon MGM Studios has not confirmed any name. Deadline says most expect a decision by the end of November, potentially before US Thanksgiving on 26 November. Treat all of this as reporting, not a decision ... ### Dante’s Inferno becomes extreme horror as The Divine Comedy wraps ... - What happened: Anxur Films, with Skincrawl Studios, has wrapped principal photography on The Divine Comedy, the new horror film from Chilean director Patricio Valladares (Hidden in the Woods), FANGORIA reported, debuting a first teaser and stills - The story: A brutal reimagining of Dante’s Inferno. Grieving writer Dante is offered a chance to bring back his late wife, Beatrice, and descends into the realm of the dead guided by Virgil, a former priest. As they go deeper, they realise something in the abyss knows exactly why Dante has come - Who’s in it: Christopher Rygh (Vikings: Valhalla) leads, with Matthew Metcalfe, Tilda Metsola and Fadhillah Othman - The tone: The filmmakers cite Clive Barker’s Hellraiser and Xavier Gens’ Frontier(s) as touchstones, promising physical horror pushed to its limits. It is expected next year - UK availability: UK date not yet confirmed ... ### Update: You Can See Everything becomes the second-biggest documentary ever in North America ... - What’s new: A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary took $8.8 million in its fourth weekend, down just 23%, and now stands at $80 million in North America, Variety reported. That puts it above March of the Penguins ($77 million) and behind only Michael Moore’s Fahrenheit 9/11 ($119 million) among non-music documentaries - For A24: It is the company’s third-biggest domestic release, behind Backrooms and Marty Supreme, on a $7 million production budget - Who made it: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim direct the near three-hour film, which follows Holmes over three years as she prepares for her 11-year prison sentence. items.title: Nerd News: Godzilla, Stranger Things & Bond (11/9/2026)
items.excerpt: ### Netflix Takes Stranger Things Into Other Worlds Netflix has announced Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure, a live-action prequel scheduled to arrive in 2028. The project comes from Matt and Ross Duffer and longtime Stranger Things writer Kate Trefry, who will serve as showrunner. The series takes place in the 1950s, before both the original show and the stage production Stranger Things: The First Shadow. Its teaser identifies the setting as Marion, Nevada, in 1955, moving the franchise away from the familiar streets of Hawkins. Joe Wright will direct the first three episodes and executive produce. Production will take place in New Mexico, with the Duffers involved through Upside Down Pictures. Netflix and the creative team are emphasizing a new setting, new characters and new mysteries.
